title: vyakarana
text: Vyākaraṇa is Sanskrit grammar, and its foundation is Pāṇini’s Aṣṭādhyāyī, about 4,000 rules (sūtras) numbered by book, chapter and rule, such as 3.1.68. vidyut includes a program that applies these rules step by step, and this module uses it to show how a written word is derived. The second section matches a word-by-word analysis of a line to the line’s written words, and the third names the sandhi rule at the join of two words.

title: vyakarana
text:
Specs and derivations
A pada is an inflected word. To ask vidyut for one, you describe it in a single string called a spec. A spec is written in SLP1 with its fields separated by |, and the first field says what kind of word it is:
s|<stem>|<liṅga>|<vibhakti>|<vacana>            a noun or adjective from a plain stem (a compound's stem written joined)
a|<text>                                        an indeclinable (avyaya)
k|<dhātu>|<kṛt>|<liṅga>|<vibhakti>|<vacana>     a noun from a root and a kṛt suffix, such as a participle
ka|<dhātu>|<kṛt>                                an indeclinable kṛt form (ktvā, lyap, tumun)
t|<dhātu>|<prayoga>|<lakāra>|<puruṣa>|<vacana>[|P|A]  a finite verb; P or A asks for active or middle endings
Liṅga is gender, vibhakti case, vacana number, prayoga voice, lakāra tense or mood, and puruṣa person, each given by vidyut’s SLP1 name. s|rAma|puM|praTamA|eka is rāmaḥ, masculine nominative singular. A dhātu (verbal root) is written <aupadeśika>,<gaṇa>,<antargaṇa>,<sanādi+…>,<upasarga+…>: the root as the Dhātupāṭha lists it, its verb class, its sub-class, any suffixes that make a new root such as the causative, and any prefixes, with unused fields left empty. t|BU,BvAdi,,,|kartari|la~w|praTama|eka|P is bhavati. dhatu turns such a field into a vidyut Dhatu, and made gives the stem vidyut builds from it: the root alone, with its prefixes set apart, or with a kṛt suffix the kṛdanta’s stem. made('Ra\\Sa~,divAdi') is naS, made('A\\px~,svAdi,,,pra', 'kta') is prApta, and a field vidyut cannot read gives an empty string.
pada turns a spec into a vidyut Pada, its noun stem made by stem, which gives a feminine in -ā or -ī its feminine suffix so sītā declines as sītāyai, not sītaiḥ, and derive returns its derivation, a vidyut Prakriya. When you also pass the written word as surf, derive returns only a derivation that ends in that word, or None, so a wrong spec gives nothing rather than some other word. derives(spec, surf) asks the same question and returns True or False. steps lists a derivation’s steps as (source, rule, result), each rule at most once while the form stays the same, with the source A for the Aṣṭādhyāyī, D for the Dhātupāṭha, U for the Uṇādipāṭha and V for a vārttika. norm prepares a form for comparison with a derivation by removing accents and writing a final anusvāra as m.
To describe a spec in words, spec_words gives its grammar in English (given the written form, a doer-voice verb reads middle when only the ātmanepada endings reach it, as kurute), spec_lemma gives the headword it stands on, and spec_root gives the root with its prefixes, such as pra+Ap. KRT and GRAM_EN hold the English names behind spec_words.
vidyut is imported inside the functions that need it, and only vidyut.prakriya is loaded, never the kosha or the segmenter. vy holds the one Vyakarana object, set to record every step.

def spec_words(
    spec, surf:NoneType=None
):
Describe a spec’s grammar in English words: the kṛt suffix’s meaning if there is one, then case, number and gender, or tense, person, number and voice.


The checks below use two words with well-known derivations. Deriving रामः applies rules 4.1.2, 8.2.66 and 8.3.15, and deriving विजयते applies 3.4.78, 3.1.68, 7.3.84 and 6.1.78. The spec for rāmaḥ checked against the written form rāmeṇa gives None.

assert {'4.1.2', '8.2.66', '8.3.15'} <= set(codes('s|rAma|puM|praTamA|eka', 'rAmaH'))
assert {'3.4.78', '3.1.68', '7.3.84', '6.1.78'} <= set(codes('t|ji\\,BvAdi,,,vi|kartari|la~w|praTama|eka', 'vijayate'))
assert derive('s|rAma|puM|praTamA|eka', 'rAmeRa') is None
assert derive('t|BU,BvAdi,,,|kartari|la~w|praTama|eka|P').text == 'Bavati'
assert spec_words('s|rAma|puM|tftIyA|eka') == ['instrumental', 'singular', 'masculine']
assert spec_lemma('k|A\\px~,svAdi,,,pra|kta|puM|dvitIyA|eka') == 'prApta' and spec_root('k|A\\px~,svAdi,,,pra|kta|puM|dvitIyA|eka') == 'pra+Ap'
assert norm('rAmaM') == 'rAmam'
assert derive('s|sItA|strI|caturTI|eka', 'sItAyE') and derive('s|nadI|strI|tftIyA|eka', 'nadyA') and derive('s|lakzmI|strI|praTamA|eka', 'lakzmIH')
kf = 't|qukf\\Y,tanAdi,,,|kartari|la~w|praTama|eka'
assert spec_words(kf, 'kurute')[-1] == 'middle' and spec_words(kf, 'karoti')[-1] == 'active' and spec_words(kf)[-1] == 'active'
cs = [c for _, c, _ in steps(derive('s|rAma|puM|dvitIyA|eka', 'rAmam'))]
assert cs.count('1.1.73') == 1

title: vyakarana
section: Placing a word-by-word analysis on the written line
text:
Placing a word-by-word analysis on the written line
A word-by-word analysis lists a line’s words in reading order with sandhi undone, so it has more, shorter entries than the line has written tokens. स कालेनेह is two written tokens and three entries: सः, कालेन, इह. align works out which entries belong to which token. It takes the tokens and a list of entries, each an object with the word in .w, such as the records from etym_entries, and returns one list of entry positions per token.
The match keeps the order of both lists. A token may take up to four consecutive entries, and they fit when their joined sandhi skeleton is similar enough to the token’s: a difflib similarity ratio of at least 0.72, scored by the token’s length. An entry that no token fits is dropped at a cost of 0.5. That cost was tuned on Gītā 4.2. Any lower and कालेनेह loses इह; any higher and विदुः takes a सः that the analysis added but the line does not have.
sandhi_skeleton is what makes the comparison tolerant of sandhi. It removes marks, drops a final s, r, ḥ, m or ṃ, and makes long vowels short, since a word’s final sound and its vowel length are what sandhi most often changes.


source

sandhi_skeleton
def sandhi_skeleton(
    slp
):
Reduce an SLP1 word to a form that survives sandhi: marks removed, a final s, r, H, m or M dropped, and long vowels made short.




source

align
def align(
    tk, es
):
Match a line’s written tokens to its word-by-word entries in order, returning the list of entry positions each token takes.



from collections import namedtuple


E = namedtuple('E', 'w')
tk = 'स कालेनेह महता योगो नष्टः परन्तप'.split()
es = [E(x) for x in ('सः', 'कालेन', 'इह', 'महता', 'योगः', 'नष्टः', 'परन्तप')]
assert align(tk, es) == [[0], [1, 2], [3], [4], [5], [6]]
assert sandhi_skeleton('rAmaH') == 'rama'

title: vyakarana
text:
The sandhi at a join
Sandhi is the set of sound changes where two words meet: ca and eva are written caiva, and rāmaḥ before gacchati becomes rāmo. join_rule takes the word before the join and the word after, both in SLP1 with sandhi undone, and names the rule that joins them. It returns (id, name, sūtra) from JOINS, such as ('vrddhi', 'vṛddhi', '6.1.88'), or None for a join that no class fits. JOINS describes 25 classes that cover the joins of classical verse, each with its Aṣṭādhyāyī sūtra and a one-line description, plus a none entry for words written apart.
Pass the written form as written when you have it. Two pairs of rules can only be told apart that way: whether the y or v of ayādi was kept or dropped (te ime written tayime or ta ime), and whether t before ś became cch (tacchrutvā) or only c.


source

join_rule
def join_rule(
    left, right, written:str=''
):
Name the sandhi between left and right (both SLP1, sandhi undone) as (id, name, sūtra) from JOINS, using the written form when given, or None if no class fits.



for l, r, w, k in [('BIma', 'arjuna', 'BImArjuna', '6.1.101'), ('mahA', 'izvAsAH', 'mahezvAsAH', '6.1.87'), ('ca', 'eva', 'cEva', '6.1.88'),
                   ('karmaRi', 'eva', 'karmaRyeva', '6.1.77'), ('karO', 'uBO', 'karAvuBO', '6.1.78'), ('te', 'api', "te'pi", '6.1.109'),
                   ('te', 'ime', 'ta ime', '8.3.19'), ('rAmaH', 'gacCati', 'rAmo gacCati', '6.1.114'), ('rAmaH', 'api', "rAmo'pi", '6.1.113'),
                   ('hariH', 'gacCati', 'harir gacCati', '8.2.66'), ('tam', 'vande', 'taM vande', '8.3.23'), ('vAk', 'ISa', 'vAgISa', '8.2.39'), ('tat', 'ca', 'tacca', '8.4.40')]:
    assert join_rule(l, r, w)[2] == k, (l, r, join_rule(l, r, w))
assert join_rule('', 'iti') is None

title: vyakarana
text:
Joining two words
join_rule names a join that is already written. join writes it. Give it two words in SLP1 as each stands alone and it returns the left word as written, the right word as written, and the class from join_rule. When the two words merge into one, as tava and iti do in taveti, the right word comes back as None.
The joins come from vidyut’s table of 1,468 sandhi rules (ganapati/data/vidyut_sandhi_rules.csv, MIT licence, in ganapati/data/LICENSE-vidyut). vidyut’s Python binding has a splitter but no joiner, so ganapati reads the table itself. A final visarga is read as s, or as r in punar, antar and prātar, and saḥ and eṣaḥ drop their visarga before a consonant by 6.1.132.

title: names
text: Readers search for names and terms in whatever spelling they know, and translations write them in yet another. This module closes the gap in three ways: one key for every spelling of a name, a table of epithets, and a table of English glosses for technical terms.

title: names
text:
One key per name
A reader may write Krishna, Kṛṣṇa, krsna or कृष्ण; Bheeshma or Bhīṣma; Venkateshwara or Veṅkaṭeśvara. name_key gives every spelling of a name one key. It applies fold_token and then the habits of Indian-English spelling: ṛ is read as ri, sh as s, w as v, ee and oo as i and u, the h of an aspirate is dropped, and doubled letters become single. Bhīṣma, Bheeshma and भीष्म all give bisma. The key is for matching only, not a spelling to show anyone.
name_key differs from roman_fold in ganapati.sanskrit mainly in its treatment of ṛ. roman_fold reads Krishna as krsna, matching a transliteration, while name_key reads Kṛṣṇa as krisna, matching the way the name is usually spelled in English.


source

name_key
def name_key(
    s:str
)->str:
Return one key for every spelling of a Sanskrit name in IAST, plain roman, Indian English or Devanagari: Bhīṣma, Bheeshma and भीष्म all give bisma.



assert name_key('Bhīṣma') == name_key('Bheeshma') == name_key('bhishma') == name_key('भीष्म') == 'bisma'
assert name_key('Kṛṣṇa') == name_key('Krishna') == name_key('कृष्ण') == 'krisna'
assert name_key('Veṅkaṭeśvara') == name_key('Venkateshwara') == name_key('Venkateswara')
assert name_key('Yudhiṣṭhira') == name_key('Yudhishthira') == 'yudistira'
assert name_key('Lakṣmaṇa') == name_key('Lakshmana') and name_key('Kārttikeya') == name_key('Kartikeya')
assert name_key('Bhīma') != name_key('Bhīṣma')
assert name_key('') == ''

title: names
section: Spellings with one vowel more or less
text:
Spellings with one vowel more or less
Some spellings still differ after name_key. Plain roman drops the vowel that IAST writes as ṛ (krsna for kṛṣṇa), Indian English adds one (krishna), and Indian English often drops a final a (arjun). name_variants looks in a pool of keys, such as the vocabulary of an index, and returns the ones that differ from a given key by a single vowel added or removed, with the same first letter. It never adds or removes a consonant, because Bhīma (bima) and Bhīṣma (bisma) are different people. A key shorter than min_len, five letters by default, matches only itself, since one vowel more on a short name often makes another name.


source

name_variants
def name_variants(
    key:str, # a `name_key`, or any key in the same form as the pool's
    pool, # the keys to look in: a set, a dict's keys, an index vocabulary
    min_len:int=5, # keys shorter than this match only themselves, since one vowel more on a short name often makes another name
)->set:
Return the keys in pool that spell the same name as key: the key itself and, from min_len letters on, keys one vowel longer or shorter with the same first letter.



pool = {'krsna', 'krisna', 'bima', 'bisma', 'arjuna', 'rama'}
assert name_variants('krsna', pool) == {'krsna', 'krisna'}
assert name_variants('krisna', pool) == {'krsna', 'krisna'}
assert name_variants('bisma', pool) == {'bisma'}           # not bima: a dropped consonant is another name
assert name_variants('arjun', pool) == {'arjuna'}          # Indian-English drops the final a
assert name_variants('ram', pool) == set()                 # under min_len: rama is not tried
assert name_variants('karisana', {'krsna'}) == set()       # three vowels

title: names
text:
Epithets
An epithet is a descriptive name for a deity or a hero: Pārtha, son of Pṛthā, for Arjuna, or Raṅganātha, lord of Raṅga, for Viṣṇu. A reader may search for the epithet when the translation writes only the main name. EPITHETS holds one group per line: first the canonical names that translations use, then |, then the epithets.
The mapping goes one way. Raṅganātha leads to Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa and Hari, but Viṣṇu does not lead to every epithet, so a search for Rāma is not widened to every Rāghava. An epithet that two figures share is in both groups, as Acyuta and Mādhava are. A name that more often means something else is left out: Śrī; Ramā (Lakṣmī), whose key rama is Rāma’s; Kṛṣṇā (Draupadī), whose key is Kṛṣṇa’s; Guha, which is Skanda but also the boatman of the Rāmāyaṇa; and Kaunteya, which is any son of Kuntī. Spellings that name_key cannot bring together are listed beside the IAST, such as Subramanya, Murugan and Bajrangbali. The names are common knowledge from the epics, the Purāṇas and temple usage, written in IAST.
canonical is the function to call. It takes a name in any spelling and returns the canonical names it leads to: an epithet’s group, a canonical name’s own group, or () if the table does not have it. It also accepts a leading Śrī, Śrīmat or Bhagavān, ṛ typed as a plain r, an English plural, and, for names of five letters or more, a dropped final a, as in Ganesh for Gaṇeśa. epithets returns the whole map from epithet keys to canonical names.


source

canonical
def canonical(
    name:str
)->tuple:
Return the canonical names that name, in any spelling, leads to, or () if the table does not have it.




source

epithets
def epithets()->dict:
Return the map from each epithet’s name_key to the canonical names a translation writes, such as ranganata to Viṣṇu, Nārāyaṇa and Hari.



assert canonical('Raṅganātha') == ('viṣṇu', 'nārāyaṇa', 'hari') == canonical('Sri Ranganatha') == canonical('Srinivasa')
assert canonical('Venkateshwara') == canonical('Balaji') == canonical('perumal') == ('viṣṇu', 'nārāyaṇa', 'hari')
assert canonical('Nārāyaṇa') == ('viṣṇu', 'nārāyaṇa', 'hari')              # a canonical name gives its group
assert canonical('Dāśarathi') == canonical('Raghava') == canonical('dasarathi') == ('rāma',)
assert canonical('Partha') == canonical('Dhananjaya') == canonical('धनञ्जय') == ('arjuna',)
assert canonical('Jānakī') == canonical('Vaidehi') == ('sītā',) and canonical('Maruti') == canonical('Anjaneya') == ('hanumān', 'hanumat')
assert canonical('Murugan') == canonical('Subramanya') == ('skanda', 'kārttikeya', 'subrahmaṇya')
assert canonical('Vinayaka') == canonical('Ganesh') == ('gaṇeśa', 'gaṇapati')    # Ganesh: the final a dropped
assert canonical('Shankar') == canonical('Mahadeva') == ('śiva',) and canonical('Ambika') == ('pārvatī', 'umā', 'gaurī')
assert set(canonical('Acyuta')) == {'viṣṇu', 'nārāyaṇa', 'hari', 'kṛṣṇa'}       # an epithet two groups share
assert canonical('Keśava') == canonical('Kesava') == ('kṛṣṇa',) and canonical('Krishna') == canonical('krsna') == ('kṛṣṇa',)   # krsna: ṛ typed as r
assert canonical('Gangeya') == ('bhīṣma',) and canonical('Vrkodara') == ('bhīma',)
assert canonical('hrsikesa') == canonical('Hrishikesha') == canonical('krsna') == ('kṛṣṇa',)
assert canonical('dharma') == canonical('karma') == canonical('') == ()
assert canonical('part') == canonical('anal') == canonical('rudhira') == canonical('ram') == ()   # English words and short stems stay out

The table is checked for one mistake: an epithet whose key is also the canonical name of a different group, which would widen every search for that name.

e = epithets()
assert e['ranganata'] == ('viṣṇu', 'nārāyaṇa', 'hari') and 'visnu' not in e   # one way: canonical names are not keys
assert not [k for k, cs in e.items() if k in _CAN and not set(cs) & set(_CAN[k])]
assert len(e) > 150 and len(_CAN) > 30

title: names
text:
Technical terms
TERMS gives the English that translations use for the technical terms of the śāstras: the means of knowledge (pramāṇas) and the categories of Nyāya, the padārthas of Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya and Yoga, Vedānta and the Gītā, and the calendar (pañcāṅga) and the horoscope. Each term has a few English glosses, the most usual first. term_gloss looks a term up by name_key, so anumāna, anumana and अनुमान are one term, and an English plural such as gunas works too. Śraddhā (faith) is left out because its key is the same as that of śrāddha, the rite for the ancestors.
A term not in the table falls back to Monier-Williams (mw_lexicon in ganapati.lemma) when you pass it as mw or it has already been downloaded; term_gloss never downloads anything. The fallback looks the term up by its SLP1 form, so it works for IAST and Devanagari but not for informal spellings, and it returns at most three glosses. terms returns the whole table by key.


source

term_gloss
def term_gloss(
    term:str, # IAST, plain roman or Devanagari
    mw:dict=None, # a `mw_lexicon()`; None uses the downloaded copy if there is one
)->tuple:
Return short English glosses for a Sanskrit technical term from TERMS, else from Monier-Williams, or () if neither knows it.




source

terms
def terms()->dict:
Return every term in TERMS by name_key, mapped to its English glosses.



assert term_gloss('anumāna') == term_gloss('anumana') == term_gloss('अनुमान') == ('inference',)
assert term_gloss('pratyaksha') == ('perception',) and term_gloss('upamana') == ('comparison', 'analogy')
assert term_gloss('saṃśaya') == term_gloss('samshaya') == ('doubt',) and term_gloss('dravya') == ('substance',)
assert term_gloss('sthitaprajña') == ('steady wisdom',) and term_gloss('moksha') == ('liberation', 'release')
assert term_gloss('nakshatra') == ('lunar mansion', 'asterism') and term_gloss('lagna') == ('ascendant',)
assert term_gloss('padarthas') == ('category',) and term_gloss('gunas') == ('quality',) and term_gloss('tamas') == ('darkness', 'inertia')
assert term_gloss('anumāna', mw={}) == ('inference',) and term_gloss('shraddha', mw={}) == ()  # the table needs no MW; śrāddha is no term
assert term_gloss('gaja', mw={'gaja': 'an elephant; the number 8'}) == ('an elephant', 'the number 8')
assert term_gloss('xyz', mw={}) == () and term_gloss('', mw={}) == ()
assert len(_TERMS) == len(TERMS.strip().splitlines()) > 120                           # no two terms share a key

The two tables do not overlap: no technical term has the same key as a name.

assert not set(_TERMS) & (set(_EPI) | set(_CAN))

text:
Facets
A facet is one field of a chunk’s metadata, such as meter, lemma or gloss, that a search can filter on. lemma_facets runs a lemmatiser over a chunk and returns {'lemma': ...} with the lemmas it found. It leaves out a lemma whose fold_token key is the same as the written word’s, because the ordinary text index finds that word already.
Some sources already carry a word-by-word analysis, and then no lemmatiser is needed. vedicreader files write it on > etym: lines, one entry per word in the form surface, lemma, grammar..., gloss, for example गणानां, gaṇa, genitive case, masculine gender, plural number, of troops. etym_entries reads such lines into AttrDict(w, lemma, gram, g) records and skips lines of any other shape. etym_facets collects the lemmas and the English gloss words from a chunk’s > etym: lines, leaving out grammar terms and common English words. It also handles two looser shapes, word: gloss entries and free English prose.
source_meta combines everything the source supplies itself: the metre facets of verse_meta and the facets of etym_facets. sanskrit_meta builds the function litesearch calls to fill a chunk’s metadata. With no arguments it returns source_meta itself, which needs neither vidyut nor its download. Given a lemmatiser, and optionally a mw_lexicon(), it also runs vidyut, but only on the chunks whose source did not supply lemmas or glosses.

text:
Searching by metre and lemma
by_lemma and by_meter are added to fastlite’s Database, so you call them on an index’s db, as in ix.db.by_meter(meter=Meter.ANUSTUBH). They filter chunks on the metadata the facets wrote and return rows with content, metadata, node_id, doc_id and page. They narrow the set of chunks and do not rank it; ordering results is the job of litesearch’s search. by_meter takes a Meter or a metre’s name, a gaṇa signature such as ma bha na ta ta ga ga, or both, and returns [] if given neither. by_lemma takes a lemma in IAST, such as gam, and finds something only if the chunks have lemma facets.

title: lemma
text:
Registering with litesearch
litesearch decides how to read a file from a profile: the extensions it covers, a test for files whose extension other formats share, the chunker, and the function that writes each chunk’s metadata. register_profiles registers two profiles. sanskrit_verse covers .xml, .json, .tei, .htm, .html, .conllu and .txt files whose contents look like Sanskrit, and chunks them with VerseChunker. sanskrit_prose uses ProseChunker; it has no extensions and never matches a file on its own, so it applies only where a caller chooses it.
You don’t normally call register_profiles yourself. ganapati declares it as an entry point in litesearch’s litesearch.profiles group, and litesearch 0.1.38 and later calls it the first time it looks up a profile, so ganapati never imports litesearch to register. Install both with pip install 'ganapati[search]'. Call register_profiles(nlp=vidyut_pipe(), mw=mw_lexicon()) to add lemmas and glosses to every document indexed after that. It is safe to call more than once.

def register_profiles(
    nlp:NoneType=None, mw:dict=None
):
Register the sanskrit_verse and sanskrit_prose profiles with litesearch, which calls this through its litesearch.profiles entry point.


The cells below check that litesearch picks the verse profile for a GRETIL file and that the metadata function works without vidyut. They then read word-by-word entries in the corpus’s own shape and in the two looser shapes.

from litesearch.data import profile_for
from litesearch import Index
import json, numpy as np
from fastcore.all import Path, first


gretil = "atha prathamo'dhyāyaḥ || MBh_1,1.1 ||\n" * 10
p = profile_for('mahabharata_u.htm', gretil)
assert p and p.name == 'sanskrit_verse'
assert p.chunker is VerseChunker and p.kind == 'sanskrit'

assert sanskrit_meta(None) is source_meta          # no pipeline, no vidyut import
# and it still carries the metre: a real verse in, its metre out
assert sanskrit_meta(None)('dharmakṣetre kurukṣetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ '
                          'māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāścaiva kimakurvata sañjaya')['meter'] == 'anuṣṭubh'
assert sanskrit_meta(None)('') == {}


# the corpus's own shape: `surface, lemma, grammar…, gloss`, one entry per line
E = """> etym: गणानां, gaṇa, genitive case, masculine gender, plural number, of troops.
> etym: हवामहे, hvā, present tense, indicative mood, first person, plural number, we invoke.
> etym: विष्णुं, viṣṇu, case=accusative, gender=masculine, number=singular, Viṣṇu, the object of the meditation."""
f = etym_facets(E)
assert 'gaṇa' in f['lemma'] and 'hvā' in f['lemma'] and 'गणानां' in f['lemma']
# the grammar fields go to neither side: the lemma already implies them
assert 'troops' in f['gloss'] and 'invoke' in f['gloss']
assert not {'genitive', 'masculine', 'plural', 'accusative', 'tense', 'case'} & set(f['gloss'].split())

# the two other shapes a source may use still split
assert 'agnā' in etym_facets('> etym: agnā: agni, voc. du.')['lemma']
assert 'dharma' in etym_facets('> etym: The compound joins dharma with kshetra.')['gloss']


# the same lines read as records: surface, lemma, the grammar fields, the gloss
es = etym_entries('गणानां, gaṇa, genitive case, masculine gender, plural number, of troops.\n'
                  'विष्णुं, viṣṇu, case=accusative, gender=masculine, number=singular, Viṣṇu, the object of the meditation.\n'
                  'तत्, tad, nominal stem, form of the pronoun, that.\n'
                  '- agnā: agni, voc. du.')            # a `word: gloss` bullet is the other shape, not an entry
assert len(es) == 3
assert es[0].w == 'गणानां' and es[0].lemma == 'gaṇa' and es[0].gram == 'genitive case, masculine gender, plural number' and es[0].g == 'of troops.'
assert es[1].gram == 'case=accusative, gender=masculine, number=singular' and es[1].g == 'Viṣṇu, the object of the meditation.'
assert es[2].gram == 'nominal stem, form of the pronoun' and es[2].g == 'that.'   # a gloss with a comma in it stays whole
assert etym_entries('') == [] and etym_entries('just prose, with commas, in it') == []

section: Glosses written in the wrong script
text:
Glosses written in the wrong script
A language model asked for word-by-word entries with Devanagari headwords sometimes writes the English gloss in Devanagari too, as though the English were IAST, so an ox; cattle comes out as अन् ओक्ष्; चत्त्ले. delatinize finds such a line and turns it back into English. It transliterates the Devanagari back into a roman scheme (IAST, ITRANS, Harvard-Kyoto or Velthuis) and keeps the result only if enough of it is English. English here means the words in gloss_vocab, the vocabulary of the corpus’s own well-formed glosses, so a word only counts if the corpus has used it in a gloss before. A correct entry and a line of real Sanskrit come back unchanged.
latin_frac gives the share of a line that reads back as English words, which is the test delatinize applies. fix_etym runs delatinize on every line of an analysis and counts the lines it changed. Transliterating back needs aksharamukha, which is not installed with ganapati; the first call tells you to install it.

title: ganapati
text:
ganapati reads Sanskrit texts and describes them in ways a search index can use. It finds where each verse ends in a GRETIL, TEI, DCS or vedicreader file and cuts the text into chunks on those boundaries. It works out the metre of every verse from the weights of its syllables, and it records the lemmas (dictionary forms) and English glosses behind the words. It also maps an epithet such as Pārtha to the name a translation uses, and it can derive a word through Pāṇini’s grammar.
ganapati is built to work with litesearch, but only the search profiles and filters in ganapati.lemma need it. When both are installed, litesearch finds ganapati through a package entry point, so a Sanskrit file added to an index is chunked by verse and each chunk gets its metre as metadata, which by_meter can then filter on:
from litesearch import Index
from ganapati import Meter

ix = Index('vault.db')
ix.add('mahabharata.htm')
ix.search('dharma')[:3]
ix.db.by_meter(meter=Meter.ANUSTUBH)[:3]

title: metre
text:
Sanskrit verse is measured in syllables, and each syllable is either light (laghu, written l) or heavy (guru, written g). A syllable is heavy when its vowel is long (ā, ī, ū, ṝ, e, ai, o, au), when it ends in an anusvāra (ṃ) or a visarga (ḥ), or when two or more consonants follow its vowel, even across a word break. A syllable at the very end of the text that ends in a consonant is also heavy. Every other syllable is light. A metre (chandas) is a rule about the pattern of these weights, usually stated for one pāda, a quarter of the verse. The anuṣṭubh or śloka of the epics has eight syllables in each pāda, and the mandākrāntā of the Meghadūta has seventeen in a fixed pattern.
Finding a metre takes three steps. deva2iast writes Devanagari in IAST and keeps the vowel length that the weights depend on. syllables divides the text into syllables and marks each one heavy or light, and scan gives the same result as a string of g and l. detect_meter then compares that string with the known metres.
deva2iast is a separate transliteration from fold_token in ganapati.sanskrit, because fold_token drops vowel length on purpose so that a search matches either spelling.

def deva2iast(
    s:str
)->str:
Transliterate Devanagari to IAST, keeping the vowel length that scansion needs.



from ganapati.metre import deva2iast


assert deva2iast('श्रीमाता') == 'śrīmātā'
assert deva2iast('देवी') == 'devī'
assert deva2iast('कर्म') == 'karma'      # the virāma kills the implicit vowel
assert deva2iast('गम्') == 'gam'
assert deva2iast('दे॒वी') == 'devī'      # the Vedic tone mark is stripped first

syllables takes IAST or Devanagari and returns (syllable, heavy) pairs. It reads an aspirated consonant such as kh or th as one consonant and the diphthongs ai and au as one vowel, so atha has two syllables, a and tha. A consonant that closes one syllable is not counted again at the start of the next: in kaṃsa the ṃ belongs to kaṃ, which makes it heavy. scan gives the pattern as a string, and mora_weights gives each syllable’s length in mātrās, the unit of duration: one for a light syllable and two for a heavy one.

def mora_weights(

Return the syllables as (syllable, mātrās) pairs, 2 for a heavy syllable and 1 for a light one.

    text:str
)->str:
Return the weight pattern of a string, g for each heavy syllable and l for each light one.




source


def syllables(
    text:str
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
Divide a Sanskrit string in IAST or Devanagari into syllables, as (syllable, heavy) pairs.



import unicodedata
from ganapati.metre import syllables, scan


assert [s for s, _ in syllables('atha')] == ['a', 'tha']      # `th` is one consonant
assert [s for s, _ in syllables('kaṃsa')] == ['kaṃ', 'sa']    # the ṃ closes the first, not opens the second
assert scan('gam') == 'g'                                     # a final cluster makes it heavy
assert scan('rāma') == 'gl'                                   # long ā, then a bare short a
assert scan('īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvaṃ') == 'gggllggg'
assert scan(unicodedata.normalize('NFD', 'īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvaṃ')) == 'gggllggg'   # decomposed IAST keeps its long vowels

title: metre
text:
The gaṇas
The handbooks of prosody describe a metre with gaṇas. A gaṇa is a named group of three syllables, and each of the eight possible groups of weights has a one-syllable name: ya is lgg, ma ggg, ta ggl, ra glg, ja lgl, bha gll, na lll and sa llg. A leftover single heavy or light syllable is ga or la. The indravajrā, for example, is ta ta ja ga ga, which spells out gglgglglgg.
GANAS holds that table. gana_pattern turns a recipe of gaṇa names into its pattern, and ganas does the reverse, reading a pattern three syllables at a time. METERS lists twenty common metres by their gaṇa recipes, the way the handbooks state them, and VRTTA_EXTRA adds eighty more as plain patterns. The recipe of every verse is stored in the search metadata, which is what by_meter in ganapati.lemma searches on.
A second family of metres counts duration instead of syllables. In the āryā and its relatives a light syllable is one mātrā and a heavy syllable two, and each half of the verse is built from groups of four mātrās. The first half of an āryā has 30 mātrās and the second 27, because its sixth group shrinks to a single light syllable. detect_matra_meter finds these metres by fitting the weights into the groups, rather than by matching a fixed pattern.

detect_meter names the metre of a whole verse. It returns an AttrDict with the metre’s name (a Meter, or None if nothing fits), the number of syllables, the syllables per_pada, the gaṇas of the first pāda in ganas, the full scan, the total matras, and, for an āryā-type metre, the mātrās of each half in halves. It returns None only for text with no syllables at all.
It tries the metres in a fixed order: first those with one pattern for all four pādas, then upajāti, then the anuṣṭubh, then the ardhasamavṛttas, and the mātrā metres last, so that a verse in a fixed-pattern metre is never relabelled as an āryā. Two rules from the tradition apply throughout. The last syllable of a pāda may be heavy or light, whatever the pattern says. And upajāti is a licence rather than a metre: a verse whose pādas mix the indravajrā and the upendravajrā. The anuṣṭubh has its own rules, which fix only the fifth to seventh syllables of each pāda, and variant says which form its odd pādas take, the regular pathyā or one of the vipulā forms.

        'yakṣaścakre janakatanayāsnānapuṇyodakeṣu '
        'snigdhacchāyātaruṣu vasatiṃ rāmagiryāśrameṣu')

                 'māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāścaiva kimakurvata sañjaya')

assert Meter.VASANTATILAKA.value == 'vasantatilakā'
assert Meter.MANDAKRANTA == 'mandākrāntā'

detect_meter needs a whole verse. Some sources give you one line at a time with no daṇḍa to show where a verse ends: forced alignment of a recording, speech recognition, and TEI files that store each line as a record. It returns the lines per verse in size, the share of verses that got a name in coverage, and the joined verses with their meters. The four lines of the Meghadūta’s first verse give a size of 4; a Rāmāyaṇa aligned half a verse at a time would give 2.

title: metre
text:
Checking scansion against a recording
A recording aligned line by line gives an outside check on the scansion. If each line’s duration comes from line_times and its mātrās from matras, the milliseconds per mātrā should stay roughly constant through a recitation. A line far from the median rate was scanned wrongly or aligned wrongly.
mora_rate gives the median milliseconds per mātrā over a chunk’s timed lines, or None if the chunk has no timings. timing_check lists the timed lines whose rate is more than tol (35% by default) away from that median, and it needs at least three timed lines to say anything. guru_laghu_ratio estimates how much longer a heavy syllable lasts than a light one, with a least-squares fit over many timed lines. The texts on prosody say 2:1. Measured over aligned Vedic recitation, the ratio comes out between 1.3 and 2.7.
The example builds timed lines from the four Meghadūta pādas at exactly 100 ms per mātrā, then slows the last line down so that timing_check flags it.

def timed(ps, rate=100):
    'Each pāda with an audio span that honours its morae at `rate` ms per mora.'
    rs = rate if isinstance(rate, list) else [rate] * len(ps)
    out, t = [], 0

assert timing_check(timed(padas, [100, 100, 100, 180]))[0].start == 8000  # the line out of proportion
assert mora_rate('\n'.join(padas)) is None              # no timings, nothing to measure

title: text
text:
Sanskrit sources rarely put one verse on one line. A GRETIL file runs verses together and closes each with a citation, a recitation text glues the verse number onto the last line, and a plain edition may have nothing but daṇḍas. verse_spans cuts a text into verses and returns each one as (start, end, text, citation), where start and end are character offsets into the input and citation is the verse’s id, or None.
It looks for one kind of marker at a time, and uses the first kind that occurs anywhere in the text:

a citation such as // Mn_1.1 //, which becomes the verse’s id;
a Devanagari verse number such as ॥ १॥, which becomes the id;
a double daṇḍa, || or // at the end of a line, which gives no id.

A text with none of these but with numbers at the start of its lines is cut at each number, and the number becomes the id. In the other cases a markdown heading also starts a new verse. A line that begins with > holds a gloss or a translation, and it stays with the verse before it.

text:
Laying out a verse
A pāda is a quarter of a verse. A printed verse usually shows two pādas on each line, a single daṇḍa (।) after the first half, and a double daṇḍa with the verse number after the second: ॥ १ ॥. Recitation sources often send the whole verse as one line, with a speaker tag such as धृतराष्ट्र उवाच (“Dhṛtarāṣṭra said”) glued to the front and the number in ASCII digits. These functions put such a verse back into the printed shape.
padas cuts one verse at each single daṇḍa, so each output line is a half-verse in the usual case. It puts a speaker tag on a line of its own and closes the last line with ॥ n ॥ in Devanagari digits. Pass num to set the number, or leave it out to keep the number the verse already carries. When you have a whole saṃhitā or chapter in one string, call split_mantras first: it cuts the text at each ॥ n ॥ and returns (number, body) pairs that you can pass to padas one at a time. A single daṇḍa before a number does not count as a marker, because the paryāya hymns of the Atharvaveda print a running count that way. deva_num writes a number in Devanagari digits, and is_word tells a word from a daṇḍa, a verse number or a stray punctuation mark.

assert padas('मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय')[-1].endswith(' ॥')   # no number anywhere: a bare close

# Kumārasambhava 4.1 across two lines with its own daṇḍas: the lines are only re-cut
K41 = 'अथ मोहपरायणा सती विवशा कामवधूर्विबोधिता ।\nविधिना प्रतिपादयिष्यता नववैधव्यमसह्यवेदनम् ॥'

# a saṃhitā blob: two mantras, numbered as written, each then split into its pādas
blob = 'इषे त्वोर्जे त्वा वायव स्थ देवो वः सविता प्रार्पयतु ॥ १ ॥ वसोः पवित्रमसि शतधारं । वसोः पवित्रमसि सहस्रधारम् ॥ २ ॥'
ms = split_mantras(blob)
assert [n for n, _ in ms] == ['१', '२'] and ms[0][1].startswith('इषे')
assert padas(ms[1][1], ms[1][0]) == ['वसोः पवित्रमसि शतधारं ।', 'वसोः पवित्रमसि सहस्रधारम् ॥ २ ॥']
assert split_mantras('') == [] and padas('') == []

# DharmicData prints AV 2.36.7's close as `॥७` with no closing daṇḍa and a newline: still a verse end, or 7 merges into 8 and `७` is left glued mid-line
av = 'अन्यं वेत्तवे ॥७\nआ ते नयतु सविता ॥ ८ ॥'
assert split_mantras(av) == [('७', 'अन्यं वेत्तवे'), ('८', 'आ ते नयतु सविता')]
assert padas('अन्यं वेत्तवे ॥७') == ['अन्यं वेत्तवे ॥ ७ ॥']
assert split_mantras('क । १० ख ॥ ११ ॥') == [('११', 'क । १० ख')]                 # a number after a daṇḍa mid-line is text, not a marker

py = 'पादयामि॥४॥ ४। १\nजितमस्माकम्॥१॥'
assert split_mantras(py) == [('४', 'पादयामि'), ('१', '४। १\nजितमस्माकम्')]

title: text
text:
Chunkers
A search index stores a text as chunks, and the chunk boundaries decide what a search result looks like: a chunk that ends mid-verse returns half a verse. chunk_verses cuts on the verse boundaries that verse_spans finds. It joins short verses until a chunk reaches target characters, and splits a verse longer than max_chars at its daṇḍas, never inside a clause. A heading always starts a new chunk. A chunk normally ends as soon as it holds a verse with a citation, so that each cited verse is its own result; pass pack_cited=True to let cited verses share a chunk up to target.
VerseChunker and ProseChunker wrap chunk_verses in the interface of a chonkie chunker, so you can pass either to litesearch’s add_doc(chunker=...). Each chunk carries start_index and end_index, its offsets in the source. VerseChunker aims for 300 characters and allows 900. ProseChunker is for prose such as commentaries, bhāṣyas and the prose Upaniṣads: it aims for 700, allows 1400, and packs cited units together. litesearch reads the chunker’s settings too, and packs text across pages only for a chunker that packs cited units, which the last two checks below confirm.

source

chunk_verses
def chunk_verses(
    text:str, # source text
    target:int=300, # pack short units forward up to this many chars
    max_chars:int=900, # split a unit longer than this at clause boundaries
    pack_cited:bool=False, # let consecutive cited units share a chunk up to `target`
)->fastcore.foundation.L:
Cut a text into chunks on verse boundaries, joining short verses up to target and splitting long ones at their daṇḍas.



from litesearch.tree import pack_target


cs = VerseChunker().chunk(two)
assert len(cs) == 2
assert two[cs[0].start_index:cs[0].end_index] == cs[0].text   # offsets point back at the source

# ProseChunker packs cited units instead, which is what commentary wants
assert len(ProseChunker().chunk(two)) == 1

# with no citation to cut on, the budget decides. 3,040 characters of daṇḍa-separated prose:
long = ' | '.join(['padam yatra tatra sarvatra gacchati'] * 80) + ' ||'
assert len(chunk_verses(long, 300, 900)) == 4
assert len(chunk_verses(long, 700, 1400)) == 3

# litesearch packs across segments only for a chunker that asks; the verse profile does not,
# because a reader that emits one verse per page is already the right size
assert pack_target(VerseChunker()) == 0
assert pack_target(ProseChunker()) == 700

title: text
text:
Reading source files
Sanskrit texts are published in several file formats, and ganapati reads five. Each reader takes a path or the file’s contents as a string and returns (pages, meta). pages is a list of (index, text) pairs, usually one per verse or section, and meta is a dict with the format, the title and whatever else the file states. When you don’t know the format, call sanskrit_parse: it looks at the extension and the first 4,000 characters and calls the right reader.



reader
source




gretil_parse
GRETIL plain-text editions, the *_u.htm files


tei_parse
TEI XML, as GRETIL and SARIT publish it


vr_xml_parse
vedicreader <lyrics> XML, which carries audio timings and a word-by-word analysis


vr_json_parse
vedicreader content JSON, which carries the same information


dcs_parse
CoNLL-U files from the Digital Corpus of Sanskrit (DCS), which give each word’s lemma



is_sanskrit answers a simpler question: whether a piece of text looks like Sanskrit at all, judged by its script, its IAST diacritics, or its citations and daṇḍas.
The vedicreader formats need a few more words. A line marked ignore="true" is printed but not recited, such as a title or a rubric, so the reader leaves it out of the text; the first line of the title section becomes meta['title']. A line aligned to a recording carries start_time_ms, end_time_ms and alignment_id. time_marker writes these into the text as [t 0-1800 a1] so that they survive chunking, and line_times reads them back from a chunk as AttrDict(text, start, end, aid, ms). A line’s translation is written on a following line that starts with >, and its word-by-word analysis on lines that start with > etym:, which line_etyms returns. The metre code ignores > lines and anything in square brackets, so neither a gloss nor a timing is scanned as verse.

Every other module in ganapati builds on the constants and functions here. They deal with three things that come up whenever you index Sanskrit: the Vedic accent marks that a search should ignore, the many ways one word can be spelled (Devanagari, IAST, plain ASCII), and the citations that label verses in an edition, such as MBh_1,1.1. None of them needs litesearch.
A few constants are used throughout. DANDA (।) and DDANDA (॥) are the single and double daṇḍa, the marks that close a half-verse and a verse. VIRAMA is the sign that removes a consonant’s built-in a. DEVANAGARI is a regular expression that matches any Devanagari character, including the Vedic extension blocks, and VEDIC_MARKS matches the accent marks alone.

def strip_vedic(
    s:str
)->str:
Remove Vedic tone marks from Devanagari text, leaving Latin diacritics alone, and return it in NFC form.


strip_vedic removes the udātta, anudātta and other tone marks from Devanagari and keeps the letters, so अ॒ग्निमी॑ळे becomes अग्निमीळे. Latin diacritics such as the macron in ā are left alone.
fold_token gives one token its search key: lowercase ASCII with no diacritics and no vowel length. Devanagari goes through deva2ascii, which writes out each consonant’s implicit a, and Latin text just loses its accents, so भीष्म and Bhīṣma both fold to bhisma. A search index applies the same key to the stored text and to the query, which is how a reader who types bhisma finds भीष्म. The function is cached, since a corpus repeats a small vocabulary many times. detect_script says whether a string is mostly Devanagari, Latin or neither.
roman_fold goes further, for names and words typed in the informal spellings of Indian English. After fold_token it drops the h of an aspirate (sh, th and bh become s, t and b), reads ee and oo as i and u, makes a vowel written twice single, reads ri before a consonant as the vowel ṛ, and treats w as v. Bheeshma and Bhīṣma both become bisma. Two options loosen it more: doubles=True makes doubled letters single, and endings=True cuts an English plural or past-tense ending. Use fold_token for text in a proper transliteration and roman_fold for text typed by someone writing English. The cell below checks each of these.

test_eq(strip_vedic('अ॒ग्निमी॑ळे'), 'अग्निमीळे')
test_eq(fold_token('भीष्म'), 'bhisma')
test_eq(fold_token('Bhīṣma'), 'bhisma')
test_eq(roman_fold('Bheeshma'), 'bisma')
test_eq(detect_script('धर्म'), 'deva')

A citation is how GRETIL and similar editions label a verse. It is an abbreviation for the work, called a siglum, followed by the verse’s place in it: || MBh_1,1.1 || is the Mahābhārata, book 1, chapter 1, verse 1. CITE_RE finds a citation between || or // markers in running text, and cite_parts splits one into the siglum and its list of numbers. A number for another edition in square brackets, as in IsUp_4[57M], is dropped.
